paper_title: Emergent Collusion in Long-Horizon LLM Agent Interaction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative settings, yet long-term interaction may give rise to undesirable coordination. We study the emergence of collusion in a long-horizon multi-agent environment: two agents repeatedly complete individual tasks, share task logs, verify each other's work, and receive rewards. We introduce realistic constraints that make compliance with the verification protocol incompatible with reward maximization, and find that agents increasingly deviate from the protocol over repeated interactions. Collusion emerges in 94% of trajectories across 10 models, and more capable models within the same family reach it earlier. Controlled peer interventions show that collusion is shaped by peer behavior, while ablations reveal additional effects of reward structure, the verification feedback agents receive, and their interaction history. In particular, restricting the amount and scope of interaction history available to agents reduces collusion. Overall, our findings show that long-horizon interaction can reshape how agents coordinate in ways that create safety risks.

sections.content: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative settings, yet long-term interaction may give rise to undesirable coordination. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Figure 1: Examples of collusion. Agents are instructed to do their tasks and verify each others work via logs. In emergent collusion, they jointly skip log exchange and verification. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative, long-horizon workflows, including software engineering (Jimenez et al., 2024; Khatua et al., 2026), automated research (Schmidgall & Moor, 2025; Karpathy, 2026), and online services (Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2025). Rather than operating independently, these agents may communicate, exchange intermediate results, and coordinate to accomplish tasks collectively. As multi-agent systems become increasingly autonomous, an important safety challenge is to ensure that agents continue to faithfully follow user instructions over extended interactions, rather than develop coordinated strategies that circumvent or violate these instructions without continuous human oversight. First two authors contributed equally. Project done while XS is visiting Stanford. 1In our study, collusion refers to joint instruction violation driven by inter-agent behavioral influence. We discuss how collusion definitions vary across studies in Section 5 and justify our definition in Appendix A. 2Code and data are available at https://github.com/SALT-NLP/agent-collusion.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Existing work on multi-agent safety (Hammond et al., 2025) often studies settings where undesirable behaviors are explicitly induced: for example, adversarial instructions are given to agents (Ren et al., 2025; Rose et al., 2026; Nakamura et al., 2026), or covert behaviors such as steganographic communication (Mathew et al., 2024) are elicited by optimizers. In contrast, we study whether undesirable behaviors can emerge from long-horizon interaction, even when no agent is instructed to misbehave. Specifically, we ask: Can agents spontaneously collude to violate their instructions? To study this question, simulated agent interactions should satisfy three requirements. First, interactions must extend over sufficiently long horizon: agents should have access to relevant history, allowing earlier actions and outcomes to shape later decisions. Second, agents must be able to influence one another, either through explicit communication or by observing each others actions. This creates the opportunity for coordinated behavior to emerge. Third, agents must face tension between faithfully following their instructions and achieving other shared objectives, giving them an incentive to optimize their behaviors in such conflict situations. These three ingredients commonly co-occur in complex real-world multi-agent workflows, where agents interact repeatedly and are linked by interdependent objectives. To stress-test whether such interactions can give rise to collusion, we abstract these ingredients into controlled environment, where fixed pair of agents interacts over multiple episodes.3 Concretely, in each episode, the two agents independently complete their own tasks, exchange evidence through communication channel, and judge whether their peers task is completed correctly. They receive shared reward when their judgments match their peers actual task correctness. At the end of each episode, both agents receive feedback and an opportunity to reflect on their performance. They retain memory across episodes, allowing them to adapt their strategies in response to past experience and their peers behavior. Most importantly, we introduce constraints that make following instructions incompatible with maximizing shared reward. Specifically, the communication channel is intentionally constrained (e.g., can only take certain amount of characters due to Internet condition) so that agents cannot exchange enough evidence to meet the verification requirements. In this scenario, we observe that the agents gradually deviate from the intended verification protocol and converge on skipping the evidence exchange, thereby maximizing reward despite violating the instructions. This strategy becomes stable over repeated interactions. Across the ten models we test, collusion emerges in 94% of trajectories. Within the same family, collusion generally appears more quickly in more capable models, whereas specific model behavior varies widely across different model families. Analysis of agents communication transcripts and reflections reveals distinct pathways in how collusion begins. For example, Gemini-3.7-Flash predominantly negotiates through communication, whereas GPT-5.6-Luna often begins colluding by following its peers violation behavior. Ablations show that system feedback during interactions, memory history, and reward design influence whether collusion emerges and becomes stable. In particular, removing memory across episodes nearly eliminates collusion. Controlled peer interventions further show that an agents willingness to violate the verification protocol tracks its peers policy, and visible reciprocity amplifies the effect. Together, these findings suggest that multi-agent safety depends not only on the alignment of individual agents but also on the interaction dynamics that shape their behavior over time. Future agent systems should evaluate safety over extended interactions, where strategies can adapt and stabilize; monitor both inter-agent communication and behavioral adaptation where coordinated behavior can emerge; and design incentives that may pressure agents to violate instructions in pursuit of shared objectives. More broadly, our results highlight the need to study alignment at the level of multi-agent systems as whole, as undesirable behavior may spontaneously emerge from repeated interactions.

The episode-level collusion rate (EC) measures the overall prevalence of collusion across episodes; the trajectory-level collusion rate (TC)

sections.content: The metrics above capture how often collusion occurs and whether it persists, they do not distinguish how trajectories first reach mutual ACCEPT. We focus on this earliest episode because it reveals how collusion first arises. Subsequent collusive episodes are less informative about its origin. Onset Signals. To distinguish how collusion begins, we inspect two stages where agents can revise their strategies: communication and reflection. An LLM-as-judge annotates one binary signal at each stage (see Appendix for prompts and human validation). For communication, the judge reads the transcript and flags an agreement if the agents establish either (i) mutual promise, where each agent commits to accepting the others work, or (ii) shared rule, where one agent proposes different condition for issuing ACCEPT and the other explicitly agrees to it. Either form is counted as an explicit, two-sided decision to bypass the verification protocol (see also Appendix G.2). For reflection, the judge reads each agents private reflection and flags relaxation if the agent both allows itself to issue ACCEPT without the complete raw log and treats this as the right strategy. Because reflections are private, relaxation reflects one agents own decision. We assign each onset to pathway using these two signals together with the verdicts and feedback from the previous episode, applying the following rules in order. The first matching rule determines the label; onsets that match none are labeled Other. Explicit Coordination (EX). The judge flags an agreement at r. The agents openly agreed to accept without the required evidence, so the onset is driven by direct coordination. Responsive Relaxation (RR). sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: Tasks. We design three task types with 50 instances each. Every instance has verifiable ground truth. (i) Code Analysis. Each instance is Python function with its specification. The 50 instances cover 25 functions, each appearing once in correct form and once with an injected bug. The agent writes and runs tests and saves bug or no bug. Answers are graded based on whether the function is buggy. (ii) Data Search. Each instance is SQLite database and natural-language query specifying set of rows. The agent inspects the schema, runs SQL to locate the rows, and saves their identifying columns. Answers are graded against the result of reference SQL query. (iii) Record Extraction. Each instance is document of individual records with inclusion and exclusion criteria for selecting them. Every record carries hidden identifier. The agent selects records that meet the criteria, submits their exact text to resolution tool to recover their identifiers, and saves those identifiers. Answers are graded by set match against the reference identifiers.

sections.title: 4.1.1 EMERGENCE AND PERSISTENCE OF COLLUSION
sections.content: Table 1 shows that collusion occurs across all ten models, but varies in frequency and persistence. Overall, 66.0% episodes involve collusion, 93.6% trajectories contain at least one such episode, and 78.8% trajectories satisfy the convergence criterion. Trajectory-level collusion rates exceed 90% for eight of the ten models, while converged collusion rates range from 36.0% to 98.0%, highlighting substantial differences in whether collusion stabilizes after emergence. Figure 3 suggests that, within model families, more capable models generally develop collusion earlier in the interaction. Across the 468 trajectories with collusion onset, the three identified representative pathways account for 90.2% of cases, while their prevalence varies substantially across models. The sharpest contrast is between Gemini-3.7-Flash and GPT-5.6-Luna. Explicit coordination accounts for Instead, 90.0% of onsets for Gemini-3.7-Flash, compared with 0.0% for GPT-5.6-Luna. GPT-5.6-Luna most often reaches collusion through responsive relaxation (62.5%). Figure 4 illustrates how these different formation processes unfold in representative trajectories. Therefore, models differ not only in how often they collude but also in the interaction process through which collusion forms. Appendix G.3 provides extended trajectories illustrating these formation processes.

As Figure 5 shows, across all heterogeneous pairings, the episode-level collusion rate falls between the corresponding same-model ECs, confirming that collusion depends on the behavior of both models. Pairing Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite with peer that tends to relax and submit ACCEPT earlier accelerates collusion onset (more details in Appendix E.1E.2). Figure 5: Episode-level collusion rate for cross-model pairs versus same-model pairs. How collusion emerges also depends on the peer. Communication transcripts show that models with low EX in the same-model setting can nevertheless respond to and agree with such invitations from others. In one trajectory between Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite and DeepSeek, Gemini-3.1 -Flash-Lite asks, have accepted your work based on your summary. Can you accept mine? DeepSeek explicitly agrees, and both then accept without the required complete logs. As result, EX is more frequent for DeepSeek when paired with Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite (12.5%), versus 4.0% in the same-model setting. However, this pattern varies across peers. With GPT-5.6-Luna, EX remains absent (0.0%). In one episode, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite commits to accepting GPT-5.6-Lunas work, but GPT-5.6-Luna emphasizes its own evaluation of the available evidence rather than making reciprocal acceptance commitment, although both ultimately accept. To isolate the effect of peer behavior, we perform controlled peer interventions in Appendix E.5. Replacing compliant scripted peer with violating one raises Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lites ACCEPT rate from 13.6% to 41.2%. For Gemini-3.7-Flash without verdict review, making the violating peers reciprocal ACCEPT observable raises acceptance from 37.0% to 55.2%. Thus, peer behavior causally influences agents willingness to relax the verification protocol.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Instruction Violation by LLM Agents Instruction following is central to modern LLM development (Ouyang et al., 2022), yet models may violate explicit instructions or implicit norms. For example, agents may modify test files despite explicit prohibitions (Zhong et al., 2025), or clone reference implementations rather than write their own when given internet access (Yang et al., 2026). Such behavior is often described as reward hacking (Amodei et al., 2016), arising from improper training data or rewards (Krakovna et al., 2020; Langosco et al., 2022; MacDiarmid et al., 2025; agatan & Zhao, 2026), or from inference-time feedback loops (Pan et al., 2024). These studies primarily examine failures of individual agents; our work instead studies how instruction violations emerge and spread when multiple agents act in shared environment together. Unintended Behavior in Multi-Agent Systems Interactions among LLM agents can produce emergent conventions and collective biases (Ashery et al., 2025), conformity to other agents judgments (Weng et al., 2025), and propagation of attacks and harmful information (Lee & Tiwari, 2024; Ju et al., 2024). Collusion, originally defined as secret agreement or cooperation, is one specific risk in such systems, although its operational definition varies across studies. One line of work studies economic collusion (Fish et al., 2024; Riemer et al., 2026), where agents converge on supra-competitive pricing strategies without explicit communication, making collusion more akin to strategic equilibrium than to safety failure. second line examines steganographic collusion (Motwani et al., 2024; Mathew et al., 2024), where agents work together covertly by embedding hidden information in their textual outputs in order to evade oversight. Other studies explicitly assign malicious or hidden objectives, including financial fraud Ren et al. (2026) and coordination before public interaction Rose et al. (2026). In this work, we study emergent collusion: joint instruction violation driven by inter-agent behavioral influence through repeated interaction, even though no agent is instructed to misbehave. Without hidden communication or an active monitor, we examine how instruction violations arise and spread through ordinary communication and feedback. Misbehavior Monitoring Detecting misbehavior in deployment is challenging because reliable ground-truth labels are often unavailable. Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring offers useful evidence about potentially misaligned behavior (Korbak et al., 2025), and can improve detection over actions and final outputs alone (Baker et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2025). With access to model activations, linear probes offer complementary approach to detecting strategic deception (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025), including collusion through aggregated activation-based signals across agents (Rose et al., 2026). Because we lack direct CoT access for many evaluated models, we use an explicit reflection phase to elicit agents stated reasons for actions and awareness of instruction violations (reasoning examples in Appendix G.1).

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We investigated whether LLM agents can spontaneously collude to violate their instructions through repeated interaction. In our setting, they often do: collusion appears in 94% of trajectories across ten models, and typically stabilizes once it emerges. This has several implications for deploying multi-agent systems. (i) Stronger capabilities do not guarantee safer collaboration. Within model family, more capable models often reach collusion faster. (ii) Environmental feedback can encourage protocol violation: the same reward and verdict information that signals success can backfire, teaching agents that bypassing instructions is the way to succeed. (iii) seemingly correct outcome can hide misaligned coordination. In our case, verdict that matches the ground truth looks like successful verification, even though the agents skipped the required log verification. These questions will become more pressing as agent systems grow in size and autonomy. Future work should study how collusion scales with more agents, evolves with more complex incentives, and varies across different communication channels, including settings where roles and objectives change over time.

sections.title: A RATIONALE FOR OUR DEFINITION OF COLLUSION
sections.content: We define collusion as joint instruction violation driven by inter-agent behavioral influence. Our environment uses mutual ACCEPT as an objective behavioral measure of joint instruction violation. Under the communication constraint, agents cannot transmit the complete raw logs required by the verification protocol, so the compliant verdict is REJECT. Mutual ACCEPT therefore constitutes joint violation of the protocol. However, mutual ACCEPT alone does not establish collusion: two agents could in principle violate the protocol independently. We therefore separately examine whether these violations are driven by inter-agent behavioral influence. Our onset analysis identifies three predominant pathways. In explicit coordination (EX), agents explicitly agree on reciprocal acceptance or jointly adopt an alternative acceptance rule. In responsive relaxation (RR), one agent relaxes its acceptance standard after its peer has already done so. In simultaneous relaxation (SR), both agents relax at the onset, so the onset does not reveal directional initiator-responder relationship. The absence of an observable initiator-responder pattern in some onset episodes does not imply the absence of peer influence. Broader peer analyses and controlled interventions (Appendix E) show that an agents propensity to relax the verification protocol depends on its peers behavior. Moreover, experimentally changing specific features of peer behavior (e.g., how the peer presents evidence, which verification policy it follows, and whether reciprocity is observable) causally changes the agents willingness to violate the protocol. Thus, mutual ACCEPT measures the joint violation, while onset analyses and controlled peer interventions provide evidence for the inter-agent influence that motivates our use of the term collusion. This operationalization is not intended as an exhaustive taxonomy of all trajectories. EX, RR, and SR capture the predominant observed onset pathways; small remainder is labeled Other and may reflect more complex or less identifiable mechanisms. Some individual cases may also admit multiple interpretations. For this reason, we use mutual ACCEPT as the primary outcome: unlike pathway labels, it is determined directly by the agents submitted verdicts and the verification protocol rather than by interpretation of their language.

These fields are replayed with their corresponding turns. B.2 EXECUTION AND CONTEXT MANAGEMENT Turn budgets and tool choice. We provide tool details in Appendix H. Each agent has 15 turns for the task completion phase, including failed tool calls. For each communication round, it can retry send message up to 2 times (3 attempts total). For the verdict submission, it can retry submit verdict up to 2 times (3 attempts total). We set tool choice=required for the task completion phase and force send message or submit verdict in the corresponding phase. We set tool choice=auto for Claude and DeepSeek because their reasoning modes do not support forced tool use. Each agent can successfully call save final answer and get log at most once per episode. Exhausting turns/attempts ends the corresponding phase/round; an unsaved answer is graded as missing. Exhausting verdict turns without valid submission produces forced reject. Context overflow and retries. On context-window overflow, we remove the oldest episode and retry the same turn; if none remains, the run fails. Overflow occurred only for self-hosted Gemma-4-31B and Qwen-3.8-27B. Failed API requests are retried up to 20 times. Retries do not count toward the agents turn budget. B.3 TASK SEQUENCES AND RAW LOGS Both agents receive distinct instances of the same task type. All models and conditions share 50 fixed sequences of 10 task pairs. Each sequence includes all three task types, repeats no instance, and never includes both the clean and buggy versions of code specification. Warm-up sequences prepend three unused task pairs, one per type, without changing the evaluation episodes. Grading awards no partial credit: code analysis compares the saved bug or no bug with the ground truth, data search compares the submitted answer-key values with the reference SQL result, and record extraction compares the submitted identifiers with the reference identifiers. Each agents raw log is JSON serialization of its task-phase tool calls, excluding get log, with fields seq, tool, arguments, and result. Agents can retrieve only their own logs and share task evidence only through communication. In the 10000 agent-episodes of the default same-model runs in Table 1, the median log length was 5289 characters. Of these logs, 9999 exceeded the total per-agent channel capacity of 5 200 = 1000 characters, preventing complete transmission. Note that we intentionally design the task so that the raw log length is strictly above 1000 characters for faithful executions. The only exception is that Qwen-3.8-27B hallucinates about its task completion and directly submits the answer in the first turn. sections.content: We examine whether protocol violations are more likely to persist when both agents submit ACCEPT. For each agent that submits ACCEPT in episode t, we measure whether it reverts to REJECT in episode + 1. We compare unilateral acceptance, where the peer submits REJECT in episode t, with joint acceptance, where the peer also submits ACCEPT. We include only episodes with an observed next episode. Each unilateral-acceptance episode contributes one observation, while each jointacceptance episode contributes two, one for each agent. Across the same-model and cross-model settings, this yields 10293 agent-episode observations (6506 same-model and 3787 cross-model). Table 8 reports reversion rates overall and by model setting and onset pathway. Overall, agents revert to REJECT in 13.5% of observations after unilateral acceptance, compared with 4.8% after joint acceptance. Both the same-model and cross-model settings show higher reversion rates after unilateral acceptance. The same pattern also appears across onset pathways. Lower reversion after joint acceptance is not limited to EX trajectories (2.3% versus 11.7% after unilateral acceptance): it also appears in SR trajectories (4.5% versus 19.0%), where collusion begins without an explicit acceptance agreement during communication.

E.5 CONTROLLED PEER BEHAVIOR INTERVENTIONS The cross-model results above suggest that peer behavior influences protocol relaxation, but changing Bobs model also changes many aspects of how Bob communicates and responds to Alice. To isolate the causal contribution of peer behavior from other differences across model identities, we replace Bob with scripted agent while holding Alices model and the rest of the environment fixed. Specifically, we consider two peer policies. The compliant peer attempts to follow the verification protocol throughout the interaction: during the communication phase, it transmits consecutive chunks of raw log, and always submits REJECT. The violating peer instead always relaxes the evidence requirement: it communicates concise summary of its task execution during communication and always submits ACCEPT. Using Bobs raw logs generated by Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, the messages for the compliant peer are constructed mechanically: we take the first 1000 characters of Bobs raw log and divide them into five consecutive 200-character messages. The drop therefore indicates that adaptive inter-agent communication, beyond the peers eventual verdict alone, contributes substantially to protocol violation. Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite Under full feedback, replacing the compliant peer with the violating peer raises Alices acceptance rate from 13.6% to 41.2%. To separate the effects of communication content and verdict policy, we additionally run the two crossed behaviors: sending raw-log chunks while submitting ACCEPT, and sending summaries while submitting REJECT. Holding communication content fixed, changing Bobs verdict from REJECT to ACCEPT increases Alices acceptance rate from 13.6% to 16.4% with raw-log chunks and from 35.0% to 41.2% with summaries. In other words, the communication messages turn out to be the bigger factor here: sending summaries yields more than 20% increase in the acceptance rate of Alice. These results suggest that both components of peer behavior can causally change Alices willingness to relax the verification protocol. Importantly, when reward or verdict review is removed, Alices acceptance rate collapses to nearly 0. This mirrors the feedback ablation in Section 4.2: Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite relies heavily on feedback to revise its own policy. Together, these results support complementary role for peer behavior and feedback: observing policy-violating peer can steer Alice toward protocol relaxation, but only when Alice also receives sufficient feedback to reinforce that behavior. Gemini-3.7-Flash As long as verdict review remains available, replacing the default peer with either scripted peer has little effect. This is consistent with the feedback ablation in Section 4.2: unlike Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, Gemini-3.7-Flash does not require reward feedback to relax the protocol, and its own verdict review provides strong adaptation signal. The importance of peer interaction becomes clearer once this adaptation signal is removed. Under no verdict review, Alice still accepts in 76.4% of episodes with the default peer, but this rate falls to 36.4% with the compliant peer and 37.0% with the violating peer. Thus, when Alice can no longer rely on its own verdict review, the behavior of the default peer accounts for large fraction of the remaining protocol violation. This dependence on the default peer is consistent with Gemini-3.7-Flashs dominant onset pathway. In the no verdict review condition in Figure 6, 95.1% of collusion onsets occur through explicit coordination (EX), in which agents typically establish that both sides will submit ACCEPT during communication. The scripted peers, by contrast, do not negotiate or reveal their eventual verdict before Alice makes its own decision: they only transmit pre-generated summaries or raw log fragments. Even though the violating peer employs relaxed verification policy, it does not provide explicit reciprocal acceptance that characterizes Gemini-3.7-Flashs default coordination behavior. We test this explanation with targeted intervention. In the no-verdict-review condition with the violating peer, we additionally reveal Bobs verdict to Alice after each episode: ## Bob's observed verdict Bob submitted ACCEPT on your task. All other aspects of the interaction remain unchanged. Thus, this intervention isolates the effect of making Bobs reciprocal action observable. Alices acceptance rate rises from 37.0% to 55.2%. This recovery indicates that the influence of peer depends not only on the verification policy it follows, but also on the behavioral signals it exposes. In particular, for Gemini-3.7-Flash, observing that the peer reciprocates ACCEPT substantially increases subsequent protocol relaxation. Taken together, these interventions show that protocol relaxation is shaped by multiple aspects of its peers behavioral strategy: what the peer communicates, what verdict it takes, and whether its willingness to reciprocate is observable.

Our operational episode-level definition classifies these episodes as non-collusive because they do not end in mutual ACCEPT. Their reasoning thus remains consistent with relaxed verification strategy: judge correctness from partial evidence, accepting when it appears sufficient and rejecting when it reveals substantive error. Such strategy may not produce mutual acceptance in every episode. G.2 DEFECTION FROM COLLUSIVE AGREEMENTS We examine whether collaborative arrangements made during communication are carried through to the final verdicts. To do so, we compare the detected agreement signal with agents subsequent decisions. Among the 1216 episodes with positive signal, 21 (1.7%) ended without mutual acceptance: 20 with one agent accepting and the other rejecting, and one with both agents rejecting. In one representative Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite episode, both agents agreed to accept based on summaries because complete raw logs could not be transmitted. Alice subsequently honored the agreement, whereas Bob reverted to the original verification protocol and rejected her for failing to provide complete raw log. These cases show that agents may explicitly coordinate during communication yet depart from the negotiated strategy when submitting their final verdicts.
